Stage 3 · Listening

What crossed the Atlantic

A talk on the Columbian Exchange, at full speed. You will not catch every word, and you do not need to.

The skill: listening for the stressed words

In connected speech the unstressed words are said extremely fast, and most of them are grammar words: articles, pronouns, auxiliaries, prepositions. The words that carry the meaning — nouns, main verbs, adjectives, numbers and negatives — are longer, louder and higher. Aim at those, and let your grammar rebuild the rest. A listener who hears tomatoes… three centuries… accepted has the sentence; a listener still looking for it took has lost the next one.

1 · Read the explanation.
Putting lessons 29 and 30 together

Three ways of attaching information to a noun. A full relative clause (the grain that is grown in the Andes), a reduced one (the grain grown in the Andes), and a participle clause attached to the whole sentence (People were suspicious of them, thinking they were dangerous). All three are common in written English; the third is the one that goes wrong most often.

When a relative clause can be reduced. Only when the noun you are describing is the subject of that clause. The grain that is grown → the grain grown. But the foods that the Europeans introduced cannot be shortened to a participle: the clause has its own subject. You may still drop the pronoun, because it is the object: the foods the Europeans introduced.

Active or passive. The -ing form means the noun does the action (the people living there); the -ed form means the action is done to it (a grain grown in the Andes). Getting this backwards produces the grain growing in the Andes by farmers, which nobody can parse.

Commas travel with the meaning. Reducing a clause does not change whether it defines or adds: quinoa, now sold everywhere, keeps its commas; a grain grown in the Andes takes none.

Which to choose. Reduced clauses make a text denser and are normal in reports and articles. Full clauses are clearer when the sentence is already long, and are safer in speech, where a listener cannot go back.

The commonest errors at this level
  • Reducing a clause that has its own subject: the foods introduced the Europeans.
  • Active for passive: a grain growing in the Andes by farmers.
  • Half-reduced: the people who living there.
  • Losing the commas of a non-defining clause when reducing it.
  • A participle whose subject is not the subject of the main clause.

Two things to watch

1 — Ask who does the verb. If it is the noun in front, shorten. If it is somebody else, leave the clause alone.

2 — Do not stack three. A noun with a reduced relative, a participle and a full clause hanging off it is grammatical and unreadable. One attachment per noun, two at most.

5 · Worked example. Read it before you do the exercises.
Deciding whether a clause can be shortened

Sentence 1: Quinoa is a grain that is grown high in the Andes.

Step 1 — find the subject of the clause. What is grown? The grain. The noun in front is the subject, so the clause can be reduced.

Step 2 — active or passive? The grain is grown by farmers, so it is passive: use the -ed form. Quinoa is a grain grown high in the Andes.

Sentence 2: These are the foods that the Europeans introduced to Asia.

Step 3 — find the subject again. Who introduced them? The Europeans, not the foods. The clause has its own subject, so no participle is possible.

Step 4 — do what you can. The pronoun is the object, so it may be dropped: the foods the Europeans introduced to Asia. That is as short as it gets.

13 · Read this before the extra practice.
Three lengths, one decision

You now have three ways of hanging information on a noun: a full relative clause, a reduced one, and a participle clause of reason or time. The skill is choosing the shortest that still says what you mean.

A defining clause reduces when the noun is the subject of the clause: the grain that is grown in the Andes → the grain grown in the Andes (passive); the people who live there → the people living there (active). It does not reduce when the clause has its own subject: the foods that the Europeans introduced can only lose the pronoun — the foods the Europeans introduced — not the verb.

Non-defining clauses reduce too, and the commas stay: quinoa, which is now sold everywhere → quinoa, now sold everywhere, · Argentina, which is associated with beef → Argentina, associated with beef,

Where compression stops

A clause of reason or time reduces only when it shares a subject with the main clause: because they thought it was dangerous → thinking it was dangerous; after it had been introduced → having been introduced. Where the subjects differ, the sentence must stay long: The crop failing in the 1840s killed a million people cannot be shortened without changing who did what.

known as, called, described as, caused by, based on are the reduced forms you meet constantly in reports: a process known as freeze-drying. Learning to read them at speed matters more than producing them.

And compression has a cost. A reduced clause hides the tense (the foods introduced in 1500 does not say by whom or exactly when) and hides the logical link (thinking it was dangerous could be because or while). Where the link matters to your argument, keep the conjunction.

Errors to watch: the foods introduced the Europeans → the clause has its own subject, so the foods the Europeans introduced · quinoa which now sold everywhere → quinoa, now sold everywhere, · Thinking it was dangerous, the crop was avoided → the crop was not thinking.

Where your food came from

Take one dish that everybody in your country treats as ancient, and follow its ingredients backwards.

The brief

Choose a dish that feels national. List what is in it, say which parts arrived from somewhere else and when, and finish with what the dish would have been two hundred years ago. Write for a reader who has never eaten it.

1 · Read the model description.
Model · a description in four paragraphs

Beshbarmak is a dish made with boiled meat and flat squares of dough, served on one wide plate and eaten with the hands. It is what appears when there is something to celebrate, and nobody in my family thinks of it as anything but ancient.

Most of it is. The horse or lamb, the broth and the dough belong to a way of life measured in animals rather than fields. What is newer is the onion, which arrived from the west, and the potato that has quietly appeared in about half the versions I have eaten, introduced barely two centuries ago and now treated as though it had always been there.

The tea afterwards is the part guests are least aware of. Tea reached the steppe by caravan, and the sugar served with it travelled further still. A table that looks entirely local is in fact dependent on three long trade routes, only one of which anybody talks about.

Two hundred years ago the same meal would have been meat, dough, broth and salt, with no potato, less tea and no sugar at all. Whether that is preferable to what we eat now is a matter of taste. What is certain is that dishes described as traditional are usually a photograph of one particular century.
